record.paper_title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges
record.original_question: How can compound-nuclear reaction theory be extended to reactions on light nuclei and on nuclei away from the valley of stability when the density of compound-nucleus resonances is too small for a purely statistical treatment, but the number of resonances is still too large to permit an individual resonance-by-resonance treatment?

evidence.quote: It has long been known that these conditions are not always fulfilled, e.g. for reactions on light nuclei, when the density of CN resonances becomes too small for a statistical treatment, but the number of resonances remains too large to allow for an individual treatment [52].
Similar difficulties can be expected for the application of reaction theories to nuclei away from the valley of stability.

artifact.status_search_result: The intermediate regime between purely statistical (Hauser–Feshbach) and individual-resonance (R-matrix) descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions remains an active research challenge. Hybrid approaches combining continuum statistical features with discrete-level features have been proposed, but no single unified, fully validated framework exists for light nuclei or nuclei far from stability. The problem appears still open, with ongoing work in the nuclear reaction theory community.

status_evidence.title: Nuclear Reaction Theory (IAEA INIS)
status_evidence.snippet: Hybrid approaches combine continuum aspects of the full statistical model with discrete-level aspects of the partial statistical model.
status_evidence.claim: Hybrid intermediate frameworks have been proposed but remain partial.

status_evidence.title: Neutron Resonance Theory for Nuclear Reactor (ANL)
status_evidence.snippet: Treatments of resonance regions differ between heavy nuclei (dense resonances) and lighter systems where individual resonances dominate.
status_evidence.claim: Standard treatments still segregate by resonance density rather than offering a unified intermediate theory.
